flashcards.q: Why do production recommenders always use a retrieval->ranking->reranking funnel instead of one model?
flashcards.a: No single model is both cheap enough to score every item in a huge catalog in real time AND rich enough to use full cross-features. Retrieval is cheap/high-recall over the full catalog; ranking is expensive/precise over the small candidate set retrieval produced.

flashcards.q: ALS: why does it parallelize better than joint SGD for matrix factorization?
flashcards.a: MF's objective is non-convex jointly in U,V but convex in U alone with V fixed (and vice versa) -- a closed-form ridge solve. Each user's U_i update, given fixed V, is independent of every other user's, making the per-user solves embarrassingly parallel, unlike joint SGD which touches U and V together every step.

flashcards.q: Why can't you just binarize implicit feedback and run explicit-rating MF on it?
flashcards.a: Absence of interaction is ambiguous (not interested vs never seen), and treating all non-interactions as confident negative ratings systematically mislabels the huge 'never seen' majority as disliked, biasing against low-exposure items/users.

flashcards.q: Weighted ALS (Hu-Koren-Volinsky) mechanism for implicit feedback?
flashcards.a: Every user-item cell is a training example with binary preference p_ij (1 if any interaction observed). Confidence c_ij = 1 + alpha*r_ij weights the loss -- unobserved cells still contribute (as weak, low-confidence 'probably not preferred') rather than being ignored or treated as certain negatives.

flashcards.q: BPR loss and why it sidesteps the missing-negative ambiguity?
flashcards.a: L = -log(sigmoid(score(u,i)-score(u,j))) for observed item i, sampled unobserved item j. Only requires a RELATIVE ranking (i above j), never an absolute target value for the unobserved item -- sidesteps the ambiguity by design.

flashcards.q: Two-tower models' single most important structural limitation?
flashcards.a: User and item towers never see each other's raw features -- they interact only via one final dot product. Cannot represent genuine cross-features (signal depending jointly on both sides), which is exactly why a separate ranking stage with real cross-features still adds accuracy.

flashcards.q: Pointwise vs pairwise vs listwise LTR -- what does each optimize, and which dominates production?
flashcards.a: Pointwise: independent regression/classification per item, no ordering objective. Pairwise (LambdaMART): directly optimizes relative order via NDCG-scaled pairwise gradients + gradient boosting -- dominant in production. Listwise: directly optimizes a full-list metric like NDCG, most theoretically aligned but harder to train.

flashcards.q: Why can offline NDCG on historical logs fail to predict online A/B results?
flashcards.a: Logs only contain outcomes for items the PREVIOUS policy chose to show -- offline metrics implicitly evaluate re-ranking already-selected items, not performance across the full candidate space. A genuinely better model surfacing previously-unshown items can show a misleadingly flat/negative offline signal.

flashcards.q: Standard cold-start mitigations for a new user/item with zero interaction history?
flashcards.a: Content-based fallback (metadata similarity), popularity-based fallback (weak generic prior), and contextual bandit exploration (explicitly balance exploring true preference vs exploiting current best guess) -- typically blended, shifting toward CF-driven exploitation as interaction history accumulates.

flashcards.q: Why does lambda (L2 reg) in MF matter especially for long-tail sparse catalogs?
flashcards.a: A row's per-item/user least-squares solve (V_obs^T V_obs + lambda*I)^-1... is built from very few observations for sparse rows, risking a poorly-conditioned/singular V_obs^T V_obs without lambda*I's stabilization -- the same mechanism as ridge regression's fix for the normal equation.
